title: The snake sheds its skin
hook: the first poem: letting go as a snake leaves its worn-out skin

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Sutta Nipata, and an old verse said aloud. Your line: old words. Today, the very first poem in that book, and an animal you might step back from.

Sometimes, on a hiking trail or under a porch, you find one: a snake's skin, papery, see-through, the whole length of the animal, even the scales over the eyes, turned inside out like a sock pulled off in one go. The snake is nowhere near. It rubbed its nose on a rough stone, loosened the edge, and crawled forward out of the old self it had outgrown. It didn't tear anything. It just left. The first poem of the Sutta Nipata takes that picture and repeats it, verse after verse, seventeen times.
screen: `A SKIN ON THE TRAIL.` → `INSIDE OUT, IN ONE PIECE.` → `SEVENTEEN TIMES.`

segments.voice: The poem is the Uraga Sutta. Uraga is a poetic word for snake, the one who moves on its chest. Every verse ends with the same refrain, which runs roughly: such a monk leaves behind this shore and the far shore, as a snake leaves its worn-out old skin. And every verse begins with a different thing let go, each with its own picture. The first: whoever holds back anger as it rises, the way a healer stops snake venom spreading with medicine. Another: whoever cuts off desire completely, like pulling up a lotus that grew in a pond. Another: whoever has broken down pride, the way a great flood sweeps away a flimsy bridge of reeds. And one of the strangest: whoever finds no solid core in any kind of existence, like someone searching fig trees for flowers. Those fig trees don't show their flowers; they're hidden inside the fruit. You'll look forever. Notice what the poem keeps saying about the old skin: it's worn out, already outgrown. Letting go here isn't a heroic tearing. It's leaving what no longer fits. Then the puzzle in the refrain: this shore and the far shore. Elsewhere, the far shore is the goal. Why leave that too? The old commentary offers several readings, one of them simply this world and the next. Some modern readers hear more: the one who's free doesn't cling even to having arrived. The poem doesn't explain itself. It just keeps shedding.
screen: `URAGA: THE ONE WHO MOVES ON ITS CHEST` · `ANGER, DESIRE, PRIDE, LET GO` · `THE SKIN IS ALREADY WORN OUT` · `EVEN THE FAR SHORE?` · then, large: `SHED THE OLD SKIN.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly: what am I still carrying that I've already outgrown? An old grudge, a story about yourself from ten years ago, a habit that made sense once. Don't fight it; just see that it's worn thin, like papery skin, and on the out-breath picture slipping forward out of it and leaving it on the path, knowing you can come back for it if you really need to.
uraga. The refrain of the Sutta Nipata's first poem: letting go of anger, desire and pride the way a snake leaves a skin it has already outgrown. Today's word.
Your line: shed the old skin. Worn out, already outgrown, left on the path. That's day five hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: The Uraga Sutta opens the Sutta Nipata and is studied and chanted in Theravada communities, and Buddhist teachers use its snake-and-skin image when they speak about letting go of anger and pride.

chat.says: Why does that old Buddhist poem keep comparing letting go to a snake?
options: A snake leaves a worn-out skin it's outgrown; letting go is leaving what no longer fits.
Snakes stand for evil, so letting go means killing the snake inside you.
Because a snake moves fast, so letting go should happen in one quick strike.
chat.meaning: In Sn 1.1 every verse ends with a snake leaving its worn-out skin: anger, desire and pride let go like something already outgrown.

Uraga.meaning: a snake, the one who moves on its chest

Sutta Nipata.meaning: the collection of discourses, a small book of mostly verse

far shore.meaning: elsewhere a picture of the goal, across the river

sources.ref: Paramatthajotika II (commentary on the Sutta Nipata), on orapara

notes: Sn 1.1 paraphrased throughout. Confirm the verse count (17) and the images: venom and medicine; the lotus; the reed bridge and flood; the fig (udumbara) tree with no flowers.
The etymology of uraga as 'chest-goer' (ura + ga) is standard; confirm stress in the 'say' field.
The commentary's readings of orapara (this shore and the far shore) vary; the script gives one common reading and says the poem doesn't explain itself.
Fig flowers being enclosed within the fruit (syconium) is botanical fact; confirm the udumbara is Ficus racemosa.
